clue.text: Like Greek poet's residence — no end sumptuous

parts.note: a residence is a home

indicators.note: no end tells us to drop the final letter of the word for sumptuous

parts.note: sumptuous means rich, lavish

explanation.surface: A description of the lavish house where an ancient Greek poet lived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' cuts the last letter from RICH, leaving RIC. 'Greek poet's' looks like part of the residence picture, but 'Like Greek poet's' is the definition: in the manner of Homer.
explanation.definitionFit: Homeric describes anything belonging to or in the style of Homer, the Greek epic poet.

clue.text: English King endlessly severe and daring, beheaded

indicators.note: endlessly means the final letter of the word for severe is dropped

parts.note: severe means hard

indicators.note: beheaded means the first letter of the word for daring is cut off

parts.note: daring means bold

explanation.surface: An English king was harsh, brave and lost his head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts HARD to HAR; 'beheaded' cuts BOLD to OLD. The king's beheading fits the picture, but it is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold II was the English king killed at Hastings in 1066.

clue.text: She was a flaming liar!

parts.note: refers to Hilaire Belloc's cautionary poem about a girl who told lies and was burned to death, so she was a liar who went up in flames

explanation.walkthrough: 'flaming' looks like an exclamation of annoyance, but the girl in Belloc's poem literally burned.
explanation.definitionFit: Matilda, in Belloc's Cautionary Tales, told dreadful lies and was burned to death.

clue.text: Dry racks one maybe used to store hay

indicators.note: maybe hints that the letters could be differently arranged

parts.note: taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Drying racks that might be used to keep hay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges DRY RACKS with I.
explanation.definitionFit: Rickyards are farmyards where ricks, stacks of hay or corn, are kept.

clue.text: Coming together with clan leader on border once, nothing given away

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here of clan

parts.note: taken as written
a verge is an edge or border

indicators.note: nothing is O, and giving it away removes that letter from once

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Clans uniting under a chief at the former border, without any concession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nothing given away' takes O (nothing) out of ONCE, leaving NCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Convergence is the act of meeting at a point, of moving towards one another.

clue.text: King drinking the wallop

indicators.note: drinking means taking something in, so one word swallows the other here

parts.note: King Lear, Shakespeare's tragic monarch
taken as written

explanation.surface: A king downing a pint of wallop, slang for beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drinking' is the container signal. 'wallop' is British slang for beer, which suits the drinking king, but here it is the verb: to thrash.
explanation.definitionFit: To leather someone is to beat them hard, the same as giving them a wallop.

clue.text: False account of the general situation

definitions.meaning: the ... of the land is how things stand overall

explanation.definitionFit: A falsehood is an untruth; the lie of the land is the way things are generally placed.

clue.text: Ban jousting in this old French province

indicators.note: in says the answer lies within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Jousting was banned in an old French region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this' is a link: the province is the one in the clue's own words.
explanation.definitionFit: Anjou was a historic county and province of France around Angers.

clue.text: Prince's friend makes start of his classic speech

indicators.note: start of picks the first letter of the word his

parts.note: oratio is Latin, a classical language, for a speech

explanation.surface: Hamlet's companion opens with a famous oration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' is a link. The Prince is Hamlet, and his loyal friend is Horatio.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio is Prince Hamlet's closest companion in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Commented about boy journalist

parts.note: re means about, concerning
Mark is a boy's name
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A remark made about a young reporter.
explanation.definitionFit: To have remarked is to have said something by way of observation.

clue.text: Silence — coldness of manner in recent upset

indicators.note: in places the word for coldness inside the scrambled letters
upset means knocked over or disturbed, so the letters of recent are rearranged

parts.note: an icy manner is a cold one, so coldness of manner is ice

explanation.surface: Someone's recent upset shows in their cold, silent manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' scrambles the word recent, and 'in' is the container signal. 'Silence' and 'coldness of manner' both look like definitions; only the first is.
explanation.definitionFit: Reticence is a reluctance to speak, a reserved silence.

clue.text: Endless mirth, spirit in the drinking-bowl

indicators.note: Endless tells us to drop the last letter of the word for mirth

parts.note: mirth means joy
rum is a spirit distilled from sugar cane

explanation.surface: A drinking party where the mirth runs out and spirit fills the bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' trims JOY to JO. A jorum is an old word, so the wordplay does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: A jorum is a large drinking vessel or bowl, often for punch.

clue.text: Find money — lie lazily — end of poverty

parts.note: to loll is to lounge or lie about idly

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of the word poverty

explanation.surface: Advice to the idle poor: find some cash, lounge about, and poverty is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Find' is a link word. LOLLY is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Lolly is informal British slang for cash.

clue.text: Come across fowl sold 'ere?

indicators.note: 'ere is here with its H dropped, Cockney-style, so the H goes from the shop phrase

parts.note: a hen counter is where poultry is sold over a shop counter

explanation.surface: A shop sign asking whether poultry is sold here.
explanation.walkthrough: The place 'fowl' are 'sold 'ere' is a HEN COUNTER, and the dropped H of 'ere tells you to say it Cockney-style as 'EN COUNTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To encounter someone is to meet them by chance, to run into them.

clue.text: Carol with lads in naughty novel

indicators.note: naughty means badly behaved, so the letters misbehave into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl called Carol among the lads in a racy book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naughty' rearranges CAROL, LADS and IN; 'with' just joins them. The novel is R. M. Ballantyne's 1857 adventure tale.
explanation.definitionFit: The Coral Island is a Victorian novel by R. M. Ballantyne about boys shipwrecked in the Pacific.

clue.text: It can be seen in Scottish range — shape roaming on crest

definitions.text: It can be seen in Scottish range

indicators.note: shape is an order to mould the following words into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something visible in the Scottish hills, with a hiker roaming along the ridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roaming' looks like the anagram signal, but its letters are needed: 'shape' rearranges ROAMING, ON and CREST together.
explanation.definitionFit: Cairngorm stone is smoky quartz, a gem found in the Cairngorm mountains of Scotland.

clue.text: Avoids team flight

parts.note: a side is a team
a flight of stairs is a set of steps

explanation.surface: A team avoids a flight of stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: To sidestep is to dodge or evade something.

clue.text: Bird on fire with love

parts.note: on fire means burning, flaming
love is zero in tennis, so O

explanation.surface: A bird ablaze with passion.
explanation.definitionFit: A flamingo is a long-legged pink wading bird.

clue.text: Wild arum from odd earl's island, possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests the words could be arranged another way

parts.note: the letters of these three words, including the S of earl's, are the fodder

explanation.surface: A wild plant found growing on a strange nobleman's island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges ODD EARL'S ISLAND; the S of earl's counts. Lords-and-ladies is the cuckoo-pint, a British hedgerow plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Lords-and-ladies is a folk name for the wild arum, Arum maculatum, also called cuckoo-pint.

clue.text: Free press 22

definitions.meaning: 22 is the answer to 22-down, a press issue, a statement put out to newspapers

explanation.definitionFit: To liberate is to let go; a press release is a statement put out for the newspapers.

clue.text: Fish and free ale distributed

indicators.note: distributed means spread around, so the letters are dispersed into a new order

explanation.surface: Fish served with complimentary beer handed round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distributed' rearranges FREE ALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Eelfare is an old term for a brood or passage of young eels, so a kind of fish.

clue.text: A Chaldean in need of immediate attention?

definitions.meaning: a man from Ur, the Chaldean city

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: a gentleman of Ur in Chaldea is an 'Ur-gent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ur was the great Chaldean city, so its man is an Ur gent; pressing matters demand action at once.

clue.text: At home among corn dealers — top-gear tradesmen

indicators.note: among means placed amid, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: millers grind and trade in corn
at home means in

explanation.surface: Merchants staying in among the grain traders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' is the container signal. 'top-gear' suggests cars, but here it means headgear.
explanation.definitionFit: Milliners make and sell hats, the gear worn on top of the head.

clue.text: Spring fruit?

definitions.meaning: to flow out or emerge from a source
offspring, the fruit of the womb

explanation.definitionFit: To issue is to emerge or flow out; issue also means offspring, figuratively a couple's fruit.

clue.text: Note god of the sun

parts.note: so (soh) is a note of the sol-fa scale
a Lar is a Roman household god

explanation.surface: A remark about the sun god of mythology.
explanation.walkthrough: 'god of the sun' reads as one phrase, like Ra or Helios, but 'god' is LAR, a Roman household god, and 'of the sun' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Solar is the adjective meaning relating to the sun.

clue.text: Approaches Northern peers, being without money

indicators.note: being without means lacking, so a letter is removed

parts.note: earls are peers of the realm
L stands for pound, from the Latin libra, so money

explanation.surface: Northern aristocrats find themselves broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being without' removes L (the pound sign's letter) from EARLS, leaving EARS.
explanation.definitionFit: Nears is a verb meaning comes close to, so it approaches.

clue.text: Friend out of condition — no progress possible

parts.note: stale describes someone who has lost their freshness or form
a mate is a friend

explanation.surface: An unfit friend can make no headway.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives the friend first, but the pieces go STALE then MATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalemate is a deadlock in which neither side can advance.

clue.text: Drunk shouts at odd intervals

indicators.note: at odd intervals picks the first, third and fifth letters of shouts

explanation.surface: A drunk shouting every so often.
explanation.definitionFit: A sot is a habitual drunkard.

clue.text: Make it too 'ot and stuff oneself

indicators.note: 'ot is hot with its H dropped, so the H goes from the word made

parts.note: to make something too hot is to overheat it

explanation.surface: A cook overheats the food and gorges on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make it too 'ot' is OVERHEAT said Cockney-style; the dropped H in ''ot' tells you to lose the H, leaving OVER-EAT.
explanation.definitionFit: To overeat is to eat too much, to gorge.

clue.text: Closely examine underworld cult

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld and the underworld itself
a sect is a cult or faction

explanation.surface: Look carefully at a sinister underground cult.
explanation.definitionFit: To dissect is to analyse something in minute detail.
